text:
Water-level declines of similar amounts are expected to occur within the Robinson Coal, Rosebud-McKay Coal, and Rosebud-McKay over-burden aquifers adjacent to the mined area on Tract III. The only significant water-level decline that has occurred in the observation wells installed peripherial to the active mine on Tract III is an apparent 5 foot decline recorded in Well 2A, completed in Rosebud-McKay Coal (Dames & Moore, 1975). Although mining has been active in the Robinson Coal since about May, 1975, no noticeable water-level decline had occurred in these aquifers as of mid-November, 1975.
Adverse effects on existing domestic and stock wells in the area will be limited to those finished in overburden, interburden and coal seam aquifers. Since most such wells are finished in the sub-Robinson unit, such effects will not be significant. Water supplies lost in adjacent areas from shallow aquifers dewatered by mining can be replaced by drilling a new well to the sub-Robinson unit. After mining, it will be possible to obtain water in reclaimed areas by establishing sub-Robinson wells.
Blasting may have some very local effects on the ground-water system by creating new fractures in the rock, particularly the coal bed aquifers (U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs, 1974, p. 124). This would tend to increase permeability and flows. This is not expected to have a measureable effect more than a few tens of feet from the blast. There is not expected to be any disruption of water between aquifers as result of the blasting.
Water Supply - Coal development on Tracts II and III will require approximately 322 acre feet per year. Approximately 161 acre feet per year
